rv.q: It's the raciest, rudest, most rip-roaringly funny show in town.
American actor Mason Alexander Park gives the funniest performance in town.
Park is a force of nature... makes her as riveting as a tractor beam.
Show is loaded with obvious jokes with American Pie-levels of puerile humour.
Some of the physical humour is worth a chuckle. But, honestly, the script and the jokes remain ridiculously thin.
That really sums up this entertaining romp: it’s a wildly unlikely sensation.

The script, and the direction of Sam Pinkleton (erstwhile choreographer of Natasha, Pierre & the Great Comet of 1812), start things off at too high a level that eventually leads to some lulls. And Mary’s character arc, while necessarily schizophrenic, could be laid out more cleanly.

Park’s Mary is riveting, and just as watchable during fiery exchanges with her husband (a no-nonsense Giles Terera), as in giddy lessons with her acting teacher (Dino Fetscher) and when bullying her chaperone (Kate O’Donnell).
It’s silly, irreverent, and utterly irresistible, full of shocks and surprises.
This imaginary version of Mary is a captivating creation – melodramatic, childish, and monstrously self-absorbed.
But that's not the same thing as living up to the hype.
This is a gloriously eccentric, rude, riotous marvel – laugh-out loud and daft as a brush.
This is not a play for everyone.
